case: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 20 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of a 2-month history of palpitations, heat intolerance, and a 4-kg (9-lb) weight loss despite a good appetite. Temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 128/64 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a diffusely enlarged, symmetric, nontender thyroid gland with a bruit, bilateral proptosis with lid retraction, and a fine tremor of the outstretched hands. Serum studies show a TSH concentration of less than 0.01 μU/mL (0.4 to 4.0) and a free T4 concentration of 3.4 ng/dL (0.8 to 1.8). Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin is present at a high titer. Diagnosis: Graves disease in pregnancy.

questions.stem: Her 66-year-old aunt also has palpitations and weight loss. The aunt's serum TSH concentration is low and her free T4 concentration is high. Physical examination shows an irregular, nodular thyroid gland and no eye or skin abnormalities. A radioactive iodine uptake scan of the aunt's thyroid gland is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Diffusely increased uptake throughout both lobes
Diffusely decreased uptake throughout both lobes
Several hot nodules with suppressed uptake between them
One cold nodule with normal uptake in the remaining gland tissue
approach: Both women have thyrotoxicosis: low TSH with high free T4.
The aunt is older, has a nodular gland, and has no eye or skin signs. This points to toxic multinodular goiter.
In toxic multinodular goiter, autonomous nodules make hormone, the high hormone level suppresses TSH, and the rest of the gland goes quiet. The scan shows patchy uptake.
questions.why: Toxic multinodular goiter develops when some nodules in a long-standing goiter become autonomous and make thyroid hormone without TSH control. The extra hormone suppresses TSH, so the normal tissue between the nodules takes up little iodine. The scan shows several hot nodules on a quiet background. In Graves disease, antibodies stimulate every follicular cell, so uptake is diffusely increased, and only Graves disease causes ophthalmopathy and pretibial myxedema.
whyNot: Diffusely increased uptake is the Graves disease pattern, because the stimulating antibody acts on the whole gland. Radioiodine is not given in pregnancy, so the pregnant patient would not be scanned until after delivery.
Diffusely low uptake with thyrotoxicosis means hormone leaking from a damaged gland (subacute or painless thyroiditis) or taken by mouth. It does not fit a nodular gland making excess hormone.
Correct.
A single cold nodule takes up little iodine and does not make the patient thyrotoxic. Cold nodules raise concern for cancer.

topics: Graves disease versus toxic multinodular goiter

questions.stem: Her thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin is of the IgG class. Which of the following is the most likely effect of this antibody on her infant after delivery?
options: Transient thyrotoxicosis that resolves as maternal IgG is cleared
Permanent hypothyroidism from antibody-mediated follicular destruction
Transient hypothyroidism from maternal IgM blocking the TSH receptor
Congenital goiter from fetal T cells sensitized to thyroglobulin
approach: Name the mechanism: Graves disease is a type II hypersensitivity in which IgG binds the TSH receptor and turns it on.
IgG is the only antibody class that crosses the placenta, carried by the neonatal Fc receptor.
Maternal IgG stimulates the fetal and newborn thyroid until it is broken down over weeks to a few months, so the effect is temporary.
questions.why: In Graves disease, thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin binds the TSH receptor and acts like TSH, which is a stimulatory form of type II hypersensitivity. Because it is IgG, it crosses the placenta. When the mother's titer is high, the antibody stimulates the infant's thyroid and causes neonatal thyrotoxicosis, with tachycardia, poor weight gain, and irritability. The infant makes none of this antibody, so the condition fades as maternal IgG is cleared over about 1 to 3 months.
whyNot: Correct.
Antibody-mediated destruction is not the Graves mechanism, and passively acquired antibody cannot cause permanent disease because the infant does not keep making it.
Some mothers make TSH receptor blocking antibodies that cause transient neonatal hypothyroidism, but those are IgG. IgM is too large to cross the placenta.
Fetal T cells are not primed against maternal thyroid antigens. A congenital goiter can occur in Graves pregnancies, but it comes from maternal stimulating IgG or antithyroid drugs.

questions.stem: Her obstetrician compares her results with those of a euthyroid patient at the same gestational age. The comparison patient has a total T4 concentration of 15 μg/dL (5 to 12), a free T4 concentration of 1.2 ng/dL (0.8 to 1.8), and a TSH concentration of 1.5 μU/mL (0.4 to 4.0). Which of the following best explains the comparison patient's laboratory findings?
options: Placental hCG stimulation of the thyrotropin receptor
Reduced hepatic degradation of free thyroxine
Greater peripheral deiodination of T4 to T3
More thyroxine-binding globulin made by the liver
approach: Notice the split: total T4 is high, but free T4 and TSH are normal, so she is euthyroid.
Total T4 includes bound hormone. A rise in total with a normal free level means more binding protein.
Estrogen in pregnancy raises hepatic production of thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG).
questions.why: About 99.97% of T4 in plasma is bound to proteins, mostly TBG, and only the free fraction enters cells and acts. Estrogen in pregnancy increases TBG synthesis and slows its clearance. More TBG binds more T4, so free T4 falls briefly, TSH rises a little, and the gland makes more hormone until free T4 is normal again. The result is a high total T4 with normal free T4 and TSH. This is why free T4 and TSH are the tests used to judge thyroid status in pregnancy.
whyNot: hCG shares an alpha subunit with TSH and can weakly stimulate the TSH receptor, mostly near the end of the first trimester. That raises free T4 and lowers TSH, which this patient does not show.
Slower breakdown of free T4 would raise free T4 and suppress TSH. Her free T4 and TSH are normal.
More conversion of T4 to T3 would use up T4 and would not raise total T4.
Correct.

questions.stem: A biopsy specimen of her thyroid gland taken before any treatment would most likely show which of the following?
options: Flattened cuboidal cells lining follicles distended by colloid
Tall columnar cells lining follicles with scalloped, pale colloid
Granulomas with multinucleated giant cells around damaged follicles
Dense fibrosis replacing follicles and extending beyond the capsule
approach: Recall normal follicles: cuboidal cells around a lumen filled with colloid.
In Graves disease, antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor continuously, so follicular cells are overactive.
Overactive cells grow taller and take colloid back in faster, so colloid is scant and its edge looks scalloped.
questions.why: Normal thyroid follicles are lined by cuboidal cells around a lumen of colloid, which stores thyroglobulin. Constant stimulation in Graves disease makes the follicular cells hypertrophic and hyperplastic, so they become tall and columnar and may fold into the lumen. The cells pull colloid back in for hormone release faster than it is stored, so the colloid is pale and scant, with scalloped edges where it is being resorbed.
whyNot: Flat cells around large colloid-filled follicles mean an inactive gland storing colloid, as in a colloid goiter after TSH stimulation has eased.
Correct.
Granulomas with giant cells around injured follicles are typical of subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis, a painful gland after a viral illness.
Fibrosis that spreads beyond the capsule into the neck is Riedel thyroiditis, which gives a rock-hard gland.

dx: Thyroid storm in toxic multinodular goiter
case: A 74-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his daughter because of a 1-day history of confusion, agitation, vomiting, and diarrhea. He has had a large nodular goiter for 20 years. Three weeks ago, he underwent CT of the abdomen with intravenous iodinated contrast. Temperature is 40.1 °C (104.2 °F), pulse is 148/min and irregularly irregular, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 152/58 mm Hg. He is disoriented. The skin is warm and moist. Examination shows a large, nontender, multinodular thyroid gland, a tremor, and no proptosis. An ECG shows atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response. Serum TSH concentration is less than 0.01 μU/mL (0.4 to 4.0), and free T4 concentration is 4.8 ng/dL (0.8 to 1.8). Diagnosis: thyroid storm in toxic multinodular goiter.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains his tachycardia and atrial fibrillation?
options: Increased cardiac beta-1 adrenergic receptor expression
Raised plasma catecholamine concentrations
Increased vagal tone at the sinoatrial and AV nodes
Left ventricular pressure overload from high vascular resistance
approach: Recognize thyroid storm: severe thyrotoxicosis with fever, delirium, and a rapid arrhythmia.
Thyroid hormone makes the heart more sensitive to normal catecholamine levels.
The cause is more beta-1 receptors on cardiac cells, which is why beta blockers control the heart rate quickly.
questions.why: Thyroid hormone increases the number of beta-1 adrenergic receptors in the heart and raises the rate of atrial depolarization. Ordinary amounts of catecholamine then produce a much larger effect, so patients have sinus tachycardia, palpitations, and, especially in older adults, atrial fibrillation. Thyroid storm is the life-threatening extreme of thyrotoxicosis, often set off by a trigger such as an iodine load, infection, or surgery. Beta blockers such as propranolol are a first step in treatment because they block this heightened sensitivity.
whyNot: Correct.
Plasma catecholamine levels are normal or low in thyrotoxicosis. The sympathetic signs come from greater tissue sensitivity. High catecholamines would point to pheochromocytoma.
More vagal tone slows the heart. Thyroid hormone does the opposite.
Thyroid hormone relaxes arterioles and lowers systemic vascular resistance, which is why his diastolic pressure is low and his pulse pressure wide.

questions.stem: Treatment includes propranolol, an antithyroid drug, and intravenous hydrocortisone. In addition to covering possible adrenal insufficiency, hydrocortisone reduces the effects of thyroid hormone on his tissues by which of the following mechanisms?
options: Blocking release of stored hormone from thyroglobulin
Inhibiting iodide uptake by the sodium-iodide symporter
Blocking thyroid hormone binding to nuclear receptors
Reducing peripheral conversion of T4 to T3
approach: The gland releases mostly T4, which is a prohormone.
Most T3, the active form, is made in peripheral tissues by deiodinase enzymes that remove one iodine from T4.
Glucocorticoids, propylthiouracil, and propranolol all slow this conversion, which lowers the active hormone quickly.
questions.why: The thyroid secretes far more T4 than T3, yet T3 binds the nuclear receptor with about 10 times the affinity. Most circulating T3 comes from 5'-deiodination of T4 in the liver, kidney, and muscle. High-dose glucocorticoids inhibit this conversion, so T3 levels fall within a day or so. This is useful in thyroid storm because the antithyroid drug stops new hormone synthesis but does nothing to hormone already in the blood.
whyNot: Large doses of iodide, given at least an hour after the antithyroid drug, block release of stored hormone. Glucocorticoids do not act this way.
Perchlorate and thiocyanate compete with iodide at the symporter. Glucocorticoids do not block iodide uptake.
No standard drug blocks the thyroid hormone receptor. Glucocorticoids work before that step by lowering the amount of T3 made.
Correct.

questions.stem: The antithyroid drug he receives is propylthiouracil. This drug lowers the synthesis of new thyroid hormone by inhibiting which of the following steps in the follicular cell?
options: Iodide transport into the cell by the sodium-iodide symporter
Oxidation and organification of iodide on thyroglobulin
Endocytosis and proteolysis of thyroglobulin to free T4 and T3
Secretion of iodide into the follicular lumen by pendrin
approach: List the steps: iodide trapping, transfer into the lumen, oxidation and organification, coupling, then storage and release.
Thionamides (propylthiouracil and methimazole) inhibit thyroid peroxidase.
Thyroid peroxidase oxidizes iodide, attaches it to tyrosines on thyroglobulin, and couples MIT and DIT.
questions.why: Follicular cells take up iodide through the sodium-iodide symporter on the basolateral membrane. Pendrin moves it into the follicular lumen. At the apical membrane, thyroid peroxidase oxidizes iodide and attaches it to tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin to form MIT and DIT, then couples them into T3 and T4. Propylthiouracil and methimazole block thyroid peroxidase, so no new hormone is made. Hormone already stored in colloid can still be released, which is why the effect takes weeks to become complete.
whyNot: Iodide trapping is blocked by perchlorate and thiocyanate. It is also the step that radioactive iodine depends on.
Correct.
Lysosomal proteolysis of thyroglobulin releases stored hormone. Large doses of iodide and lithium slow this step.
Pendrin moves iodide across the apical membrane into the lumen. Its genetic loss causes Pendred syndrome (goiter with deafness), and thionamides do not target it.

questions.stem: On examination, his nodular neck mass rises when he swallows. Which of the following best explains this movement?
options: Enclosure within the carotid sheath beside the larynx
Suspension from the hyoid bone by the infrahyoid muscles
Pretracheal fascia binding it to the laryngeal cartilages
Fixation to the prevertebral fascia over the vertebral bodies
approach: Locate the gland: the lobes lie beside the larynx and trachea, and the isthmus crosses the second and third tracheal rings.
The gland is wrapped in the pretracheal layer of deep cervical fascia, which attaches to the thyroid and cricoid cartilages.
The larynx rises during swallowing, so the thyroid and any mass in it rise too.
questions.why: The thyroid sits in the pretracheal (visceral) fascia, which is attached above to the thyroid and cricoid cartilages. Dense ligaments also bind the gland to the cricoid cartilage and upper tracheal rings. When the larynx moves up during swallowing, the thyroid moves with it. A neck mass that rises on swallowing is therefore likely to be in the thyroid gland.
whyNot: The carotid sheath holds the common carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve lateral to the thyroid. It is not attached to the larynx and does not carry the gland upward.
The infrahyoid (strap) muscles lie in front of the thyroid but do not suspend it. Their own movement does not explain why a mass inside the gland rises.
Correct.
Prevertebral fascia covers the vertebral column and the muscles on it. A structure fixed there would stay still during swallowing.

case: A 46-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, heavy menses, and a 5-kg (11-lb) weight gain. She has vitiligo. Temperature is 36.2 °C (97.2 °F), pulse is 56/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 132/86 mm Hg. Physical examination shows dry, coarse skin and a diffusely enlarged, firm, rubbery, nontender thyroid gland. The relaxation phase of the ankle reflexes is delayed. Serum studies show a TSH concentration of 24 μU/mL (0.4 to 4.0), a free T4 concentration of 0.5 ng/dL (0.8 to 1.8), and an anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody titer of 640 IU/mL (less than 35). Diagnosis: Hashimoto thyroiditis with primary hypothyroidism.

questions.stem: A core biopsy specimen of her thyroid gland is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Granulomas with multinucleated giant cells around leaked colloid
Hyperplastic follicles lined by tall columnar cells
Dense fibrosis extending into the adjacent strap muscles
Lymphoid follicles with germinal centers and Hürthle cells
approach: Identify the disease: painless, rubbery goiter in a middle-aged woman with hypothyroidism and anti-TPO antibodies is Hashimoto thyroiditis.
The gland is the site of an ongoing autoimmune reaction, so it fills with lymphocytes and plasma cells, which form germinal centers.
Surviving follicular cells change into Hürthle cells, with pink granular cytoplasm packed with mitochondria.
questions.why: In Hashimoto thyroiditis, tolerance to thyroid antigens is lost. T cells and B cells invade the gland and organize into lymphoid follicles with germinal centers, as in a lymph node. Follicles shrink and are destroyed. Remaining follicular cells become Hürthle (oxyphil) cells with abundant eosinophilic, granular cytoplasm. The infiltrate enlarges the gland, so it is firm and painless while its function slowly fails.
whyNot: Granulomas with giant cells around colloid describe subacute granulomatous thyroiditis, which causes a painful, tender gland after a viral illness.
Tall columnar cells in hyperplastic follicles mean an overstimulated gland, as in Graves disease, the opposite of her hypothyroid state.
Fibrosis that extends beyond the capsule into the strap muscles is Riedel thyroiditis. In Hashimoto thyroiditis any fibrosis stays inside the capsule.
Correct.

questions.stem: She is treated with levothyroxine. Nine years later, she notes painless enlargement of the thyroid gland over 6 weeks, with hoarseness and difficulty swallowing. Which of the following neoplasms is most likely?
options: Medullary carcinoma from C cells
Primary B-cell lymphoma
Follicular carcinoma
Parathyroid carcinoma
approach: Note the setting: long-standing Hashimoto thyroiditis, then a rapidly enlarging gland that compresses nearby structures.
Years of lymphoid stimulation in the gland raise the risk of a B-cell clone escaping control.
This makes primary thyroid B-cell lymphoma the classic tumor linked to Hashimoto thyroiditis.
questions.why: Hashimoto thyroiditis usually moves from a possible brief thyrotoxic phase, as follicles break down, to permanent hypothyroidism. It also clusters with other autoimmune diseases, such as vitiligo, type 1 diabetes, and pernicious anemia. The gland contains lymphoid tissue that is chronically stimulated by antigen, and this raises the risk of primary thyroid B-cell lymphoma, often marginal zone (MALT) or diffuse large B-cell type. The usual presentation is rapid, painless growth in a middle-aged or older woman with Hashimoto thyroiditis.
whyNot: Medullary carcinoma arises from calcitonin-secreting C cells. It is linked to RET mutations and MEN 2, not to autoimmune thyroiditis.
Correct.
Follicular carcinoma usually presents as a solitary nodule and spreads by blood to bone and lung. It is not associated with Hashimoto thyroiditis.
Parathyroid carcinoma is rare, causes marked hypercalcemia, and is unrelated to thyroid autoimmunity.

questions.stem: Which of the following immune mechanisms is chiefly responsible for the loss of her thyroid follicular cells?
options: CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell killing of follicular cells
Antibody stimulation of the thyrotropin receptor
IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation in the gland
Granulomatous response to colloid after viral injury
approach: Her anti-TPO antibodies show autoimmunity against the thyroid, but they are mainly a diagnostic marker.
The main damage in Hashimoto thyroiditis comes from cell-mediated immunity.
Cytotoxic CD8+ T cells kill follicular cells, helped by cytokines such as interferon gamma from CD4+ T cells.
questions.why: Hashimoto thyroiditis is driven mainly by T cells. CD8+ cytotoxic T cells recognize thyroid antigens and kill follicular cells. CD4+ helper T cells release interferon gamma, which activates macrophages and adds to the injury. Antibodies against thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulin are present in most patients and are the main laboratory marker, and they may add some antibody-dependent killing. A high anti-TPO titer supports the diagnosis and predicts progression to hypothyroidism.
whyNot: Correct.
Antibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor cause Graves disease and hyperthyroidism, not follicle loss.
IgE and mast cells mediate type I hypersensitivity, such as allergy and anaphylaxis. They play no role in autoimmune thyroiditis.
A granulomatous reaction to leaked colloid after a viral infection is the mechanism of subacute granulomatous thyroiditis, which is self-limited.

questions.stem: After she starts levothyroxine, her fatigue improves only gradually over several weeks, whereas an injection of epinephrine raises heart rate within seconds. Which of the following best explains the slower onset of thyroid hormone action?
options: It must first be stored as colloid within the thyroid follicles
It acts through a G protein-coupled receptor that generates cAMP
It changes gene transcription through a nuclear receptor
It opens ligand-gated ion channels in the target cell membrane
approach: Compare receptor types: epinephrine binds membrane receptors that change enzyme activity within seconds.
T3 enters the cell and binds a receptor in the nucleus that is a transcription factor.
New mRNA and protein must be made before the effect appears, which takes hours to days. The long half-life of T4 (about 7 days) also means levels take weeks to reach a steady state.
questions.why: The thyroid hormone receptor sits in the nucleus bound to thyroid hormone response elements in DNA, usually as a heterodimer with the retinoid X receptor. When T3 binds, the receptor releases corepressors, recruits coactivators, and changes transcription of target genes such as Na/K-ATPase and beta-1 adrenergic receptors. Effects that depend on making new proteins develop over hours to days. Peptide hormones and catecholamines act through membrane receptors and second messengers that modify existing proteins, so they act within seconds to minutes.
whyNot: Levothyroxine is absorbed from the gut into the blood and acts directly on tissues. Colloid storage happens only in the thyroid, which is failing in this patient.
Gs-coupled receptors with cAMP are used by TSH, glucagon, and beta-adrenergic agonists. They act quickly.
Correct.
Ligand-gated ion channels, such as the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, respond within milliseconds.

case: A 38-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 5-day history of pain in the front of her neck that radiates to both ears, with fever and palpitations. Two weeks ago, she had a sore throat, rhinorrhea, and cough that resolved without treatment. Temperature is 38.3 °C (100.9 °F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 126/78 mm Hg. The thyroid gland is slightly enlarged, firm, and exquisitely tender. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 78 mm/h (0 to 20). Serum TSH concentration is 0.05 μU/mL (0.4 to 4.0), and free T4 concentration is 2.6 ng/dL (0.8 to 1.8). The 24-hour radioactive iodine uptake is 2% (10 to 30). Diagnosis: subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her high free T4 concentration together with a low radioactive iodine uptake?
options: Antibodies that block the thyrotropin receptor
Release of preformed hormone from injured follicles
Autonomous hormone synthesis by a follicular adenoma
Stimulation of the gland by circulating hCG
approach: Uptake measures how actively the gland is making new hormone.
High hormone with low uptake means the hormone is not newly made. It is leaking from a damaged gland, or it is being taken by mouth.
A painful, tender gland with fever and a high ESR after a viral illness points to inflammatory destruction of follicles.
questions.why: In subacute granulomatous thyroiditis, inflammation breaks open follicles, and stored T4 and T3 spill into the blood. The patient becomes thyrotoxic, and the high hormone level suppresses TSH. Without TSH, and with follicular cells injured, the gland traps very little iodine, so uptake is low. The tender gland, fever, and raised ESR separate this from painless forms. Histology shows granulomas with multinucleated giant cells around fragments of colloid.
whyNot: Blocking antibodies to the TSH receptor reduce thyroid function and would cause hypothyroidism, not thyrotoxicosis.
Correct.
An autonomous adenoma makes new hormone and shows a hot nodule with high uptake. It does not cause fever or a tender gland.
hCG stimulates the TSH receptor in early pregnancy or with molar pregnancy. It increases hormone synthesis, so uptake would be high.

questions.stem: Which of the following infectious agents has been implicated as a trigger of her condition?
options: Staphylococcus aureus
Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Coxsackievirus
Streptococcus pyogenes
approach: Note the timing: a cold with rhinorrhea and cough 2 weeks before the thyroid pain.
Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis follows viral upper respiratory infections, and the gland itself is not infected by bacteria.
Viruses linked to it include coxsackievirus, mumps virus, and adenovirus.
questions.why: Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis usually begins 2 to 8 weeks after a viral upper respiratory infection. Coxsackievirus, mumps virus, measles virus, and adenovirus have been implicated. It is thought that viral injury or a cross-reacting immune response damages follicular cells, and the granulomas form around leaked colloid. It is more common in women in their 30s to 50s and follows a seasonal pattern like that of viral infections.
whyNot: Staphylococcus aureus causes acute suppurative thyroiditis, a bacterial infection with a tender, sometimes fluctuant gland and usually normal thyroid function.
Tuberculosis of the thyroid is rare and forms caseating granulomas. The granulomas of de Quervain thyroiditis are noncaseating and form around colloid.
Correct.
Streptococcus pyogenes can infect the thyroid directly in acute suppurative thyroiditis. Her preceding illness, with rhinorrhea and cough, suggests a virus.

questions.stem: If she is followed without antithyroid drugs, which of the following sequences of thyroid function is most likely over the next 6 months?
options: Thyrotoxicosis, then transient hypothyroidism, then normal function
Thyrotoxicosis that persists until the gland is ablated
Thyrotoxicosis, then permanent hypothyroidism needing lifelong treatment
Normal function for months, then recurrent thyrotoxicosis
approach: The gland is releasing a fixed store of hormone from damaged follicles.
Once that store is used up, and while follicles are still injured, hormone levels fall below normal for a while.
As inflammation settles, follicles regenerate and function returns to normal in most patients.
questions.why: The thyrotoxic phase lasts a few weeks, until stored colloid is exhausted. A hypothyroid phase often follows, lasting weeks to a few months, because the injured gland cannot yet make enough hormone. Over about 6 to 12 months most patients recover normal function, and only a small share stay hypothyroid. Antithyroid drugs do not help because they block synthesis, and the problem is leakage of hormone already made. Beta blockers and anti-inflammatory drugs treat symptoms.
whyNot: Correct.
Ongoing thyrotoxicosis needing ablation fits Graves disease or a toxic nodule, where the gland keeps making new hormone.
Permanent hypothyroidism is the usual end of Hashimoto thyroiditis. It is uncommon after subacute thyroiditis.
Recurrence happens in a few patients, but the typical course is a single episode that resolves.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man has a slowly enlarging, painless, rock-hard thyroid gland that is fixed to the trachea and strap muscles. He has hoarseness and stridor, and CT of the abdomen shows retroperitoneal fibrosis. Thyroid function is normal. A biopsy specimen of his thyroid gland is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Granulomas around fragments of colloid with giant cells
Lymphoid germinal centers with oxyphilic Hürthle cells
Hyperplastic follicles lined by tall columnar cells
Dense fibrosis with many IgG4-positive plasma cells
approach: Notice the differences from the case: no pain, no thyrotoxicosis, and a hard gland fixed to nearby structures.
Fibrosis that invades outside the gland, together with retroperitoneal fibrosis, points to Riedel thyroiditis.
Riedel thyroiditis is often part of IgG4-related disease.
questions.why: Riedel thyroiditis replaces the gland with dense fibrous tissue that extends through the capsule into the trachea, esophagus, strap muscles, and nerves. The hard, fixed gland can mimic cancer and cause stridor, dysphagia, or hoarseness. Many cases belong to IgG4-related disease, with IgG4-positive plasma cells and fibrosis at other sites, such as the retroperitoneum. Painless (silent) and postpartum thyroiditis are different again: they are lymphocytic, cause brief thyrotoxicosis with low uptake, and have no pain or fibrosis.
whyNot: Granulomas around colloid are the histology of subacute granulomatous thyroiditis, which is painful and causes transient thyrotoxicosis.
Germinal centers and Hürthle cells are typical of Hashimoto thyroiditis. Its fibrosing form stays within the thyroid capsule.
Tall columnar hyperplastic cells mean an overstimulated gland, as in Graves disease, which is not rock-hard or fixed.
Correct.

case: A 34-year-old woman who recently moved from a remote mountain village in Nepal comes to the physician because of neck swelling for several years and a 1-year history of fatigue, cold intolerance, and weight gain. Her family cooked with uniodized rock salt. Temperature is 36.1 °C (97.0 °F), pulse is 54/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 128/84 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a large, nontender goiter with several palpable nodules and delayed relaxation of the ankle reflexes. Serum studies show a TSH concentration of 38 μU/mL (0.4 to 4.0), a free T4 concentration of 0.4 ng/dL (0.8 to 1.8), negative anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies, and an LDL-cholesterol concentration of 182 mg/dL (less than 100). Urinary iodine concentration is 22 μg/L (100 or more). Diagnosis: iodine deficiency goiter with hypothyroidism.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her increased serum LDL-cholesterol concentration?
options: Increased hepatic secretion of VLDL
Absence of apolipoprotein C-II on chylomicrons
Fewer LDL receptors on hepatocytes
Increased intestinal absorption of cholesterol
approach: Link the lipid change to her low thyroid hormone level.
Thyroid hormone increases transcription of the LDL receptor gene in the liver.
With less thyroid hormone, the liver clears less LDL from the blood, so LDL rises.
questions.why: T3 increases the number of LDL receptors on hepatocytes. In hypothyroidism, fewer receptors means slower clearance of LDL, so total and LDL cholesterol rise, and the hyperlipidemia improves with thyroid hormone replacement. The same low metabolic state explains her other signs: less heat production causes cold intolerance, less beta-adrenergic sensitivity causes bradycardia, and slower muscle contraction and relaxation cause the delayed reflex relaxation phase. Her goiter comes from chronically high TSH stimulating the gland.
whyNot: More VLDL secretion raises triglycerides and is seen with insulin resistance and alcohol use. It is not the main lipid change in hypothyroidism.
Loss of apolipoprotein C-II prevents lipoprotein lipase from clearing chylomicrons and causes very high triglycerides (type I hyperlipoproteinemia).
Correct.
Cholesterol absorption in the gut is not driven by thyroid hormone status.

questions.stem: Her village diet is also low in selenium. A deficiency of this trace element would most directly impair which of the following steps in thyroid hormone metabolism?
options: Uptake of iodide by the sodium-iodide symporter
Coupling of iodotyrosines by thyroid peroxidase
Proteolysis of thyroglobulin in lysosomes
Conversion of T4 to T3 by deiodinases
approach: Recall which enzymes need selenium: deiodinases and glutathione peroxidase are selenoproteins.
Deiodinases remove iodine from T4 to make active T3.
Selenium deficiency therefore reduces formation of T3 in tissues and adds to the effects of iodine deficiency.
questions.why: Iodine is built into the hormone itself, so a shortage limits how much T4 and T3 the gland can make. Free T4 falls, TSH rises by negative feedback, and the gland enlarges. Selenium is needed for a different step. The iodothyronine deiodinases contain selenocysteine at the active site and convert T4 to T3 in peripheral tissues. Selenium also supports glutathione peroxidase, which protects the thyroid from the hydrogen peroxide used in hormone synthesis.
whyNot: The sodium-iodide symporter is driven by the sodium gradient from Na/K-ATPase and needs no selenium. Its activity rises in iodine deficiency because TSH is high.
Thyroid peroxidase is a heme enzyme that uses hydrogen peroxide. It does not contain selenium.
Thyroglobulin is broken down by lysosomal proteases after endocytosis. This step does not depend on selenium.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her 41-year-old sister has fatigue and cold intolerance. Two years ago, the sister had severe postpartum hemorrhage and was unable to breastfeed afterward. The sister's free T4 concentration is 0.5 ng/dL (0.8 to 1.8), her TSH concentration is 0.6 μU/mL (0.4 to 4.0), and her 8 AM serum cortisol and plasma ACTH concentrations are both low. Which of the following is the most likely site of the sister's disorder?
options: Thyroid follicular epithelium
Anterior pituitary gland
Posterior pituitary gland
Adrenal cortex
approach: Pair each target hormone with its trophic hormone: low free T4 with a TSH that is not raised, and low cortisol with low ACTH.
If the target gland were failing, the trophic hormones would rise by negative feedback. Low or normal trophic hormones point higher up the axis.
Two axes failing together after postpartum hemorrhage and failed lactation points to the anterior pituitary (Sheehan syndrome).
questions.why: Negative feedback lets you localize an endocrine problem. In primary hypothyroidism, as in the patient, low free T4 removes feedback, so TSH rises sharply. In the sister, TSH stays in the normal range even though free T4 is low, which means the pituitary cannot respond. Low cortisol with low ACTH shows the same pattern in the adrenal axis. The pituitary enlarges in pregnancy, and severe postpartum hemorrhage can cause ischemic necrosis of the anterior lobe. Loss of prolactin explains her failure to lactate.
whyNot: Primary thyroid failure would raise TSH by loss of negative feedback, as in the woman with iodine deficiency goiter.
Correct.
The posterior pituitary releases ADH and oxytocin. Its loss causes diabetes insipidus and does not lower TSH or ACTH.
Primary adrenal failure would raise ACTH and would not explain low free T4 with a normal TSH.

questions.stem: After treatment, she undergoes thyroidectomy because the goiter compresses her trachea. While mobilizing the lower part of the left lobe, the surgeon ligates an artery that enters the posterior surface of the gland after passing medially behind the carotid sheath. This artery most likely arises from which of the following?
options: Thyrocervical trunk
External carotid artery
Brachiocephalic trunk
Internal thoracic artery
approach: Identify the vessel: an artery reaching the lower posterior gland from behind the carotid sheath is the inferior thyroid artery.
Recall its origin: the thyrocervical trunk, a branch of the first part of the subclavian artery.
Contrast it with the superior thyroid artery, which comes from the external carotid and enters the upper pole.
questions.why: The thyroid has two main paired arteries. The superior thyroid artery is the first branch of the external carotid artery and reaches the upper pole. The inferior thyroid artery comes from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery, runs up and then medially behind the carotid sheath, and enters the posterior gland near the lower pole. In some people a small thyroid ima artery rises from the brachiocephalic trunk or aortic arch to the isthmus. Veins drain through the superior and middle thyroid veins to the internal jugular vein and through the inferior thyroid veins to the brachiocephalic veins.
whyNot: Correct.
The external carotid artery gives the superior thyroid artery, which supplies the upper pole and travels with the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.
The brachiocephalic trunk is the usual source of the inconstant thyroid ima artery, which reaches the isthmus from below in the midline.
The internal thoracic artery runs down behind the anterior chest wall and does not supply the thyroid.

dx: Congenital hypothyroidism from thyroid dysgenesis (lingual thyroid)
case: A 3-week-old girl born at term is brought to the physician after her newborn screening test showed a high TSH concentration. Her parents report that she is sleepy, feeds poorly, and has remained jaundiced. Temperature is 36.2 °C (97.2 °F), pulse is 104/min, and respirations are 34/min. Physical examination shows jaundice, a large protruding tongue, a wide posterior fontanelle, and an umbilical hernia. No thyroid tissue is palpable in the neck. Serum TSH concentration is 85 μU/mL (reference for age, less than 10), and free T4 concentration is 0.5 ng/dL (reference for age, 0.9 to 2.2). A technetium-99m thyroid scan shows no tissue in the normal position and a small focus of uptake at the base of the tongue. Diagnosis: congenital hypothyroidism from thyroid dysgenesis (lingual thyroid).

questions.stem: If thyroid hormone replacement were delayed for several months, which of the following outcomes would be most likely?
options: Permanent intellectual disability and short stature
Accelerated bone age with early closure of growth plates
Recurrent hypoglycemic seizures from excess insulin
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with heart failure
approach: Recognize the signs of congenital hypothyroidism: lethargy, poor feeding, prolonged jaundice, large tongue, wide fontanelle, umbilical hernia.
Thyroid hormone is required for brain maturation and skeletal growth in the first years of life.
Without early treatment, the brain damage is permanent and growth is stunted.
questions.why: Thyroid hormone drives neuronal growth, synapse formation, and myelination in the first 2 to 3 years of life, and it is needed for normal bone growth and maturation. Untreated congenital hypothyroidism causes permanent intellectual disability and short stature with delayed bone age. Newborn screening exists because most affected infants look normal at birth, and treatment started within the first 2 weeks gives normal or near-normal development. Thyroid dysgenesis (absent, small, or ectopic gland) is the most common cause, followed by dyshormonogenesis. Maternal iodine deficiency is the leading cause worldwide.
whyNot: Correct.
Hypothyroidism delays bone age. Accelerated bone age with early growth plate closure suggests excess sex steroids or thyroid hormone.
Hypoglycemic seizures from excess insulin fit congenital hyperinsulinism or an infant of a diabetic mother, not hypothyroidism.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is linked to sarcomere gene mutations and infants of diabetic mothers. Hypothyroidism causes bradycardia and sometimes pericardial effusion.

questions.stem: Which of the following embryologic events best explains the location of her thyroid tissue?
options: Persistence of the second pharyngeal cleft
Failed descent from the foramen cecum
Migration with the third pharyngeal pouch
Abnormal fusion of the lateral lingual swellings
approach: Recall where the thyroid begins: an endodermal outgrowth at the foramen cecum, at the junction of the anterior two thirds and posterior third of the tongue.
The gland descends in front of the hyoid bone and larynx along the thyroglossal duct to reach the lower neck by about week 7.
Tissue that never leaves its starting point remains at the base of the tongue as a lingual thyroid.
questions.why: The thyroid starts in week 4 as a midline thickening of endoderm in the floor of the pharynx, marked later by the foramen cecum of the tongue. It grows down as a bilobed diverticulum, stays attached by the thyroglossal duct, passes in front of the hyoid bone, and reaches its final position in front of the trachea. If descent fails, the gland stays at the base of the tongue. A lingual thyroid is often the only thyroid tissue present and is often too small to make enough hormone, as in this infant.
whyNot: A persistent second pharyngeal cleft forms a lateral branchial cleft cyst or sinus along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid. It does not contain thyroid tissue.
Correct.
The third pharyngeal pouch forms the thymus and inferior parathyroid glands, which may end up ectopic in the mediastinum. It is not the source of thyroid follicular cells.
The lateral lingual swellings form the anterior two thirds of the tongue. Their fusion does not determine where thyroid tissue lies.

questions.stem: TSH stimulates hormone synthesis and growth in her small amount of functioning thyroid tissue. Binding of TSH to its receptor on follicular cells signals mainly through which of the following pathways?
options: Intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity of the receptor
JAK2 kinase activation of STAT transcription factors
Gq-coupled phospholipase C with IP3 and calcium
Gs-coupled adenylyl cyclase and cAMP
approach: TSH is a glycoprotein hormone from the anterior pituitary, like LH and FSH.
These hormones bind G protein-coupled receptors linked to Gs.
Gs activates adenylyl cyclase, cAMP activates protein kinase A, and this raises iodide uptake, hormone synthesis, and gland growth.
questions.why: The TSH receptor is a G protein-coupled receptor. Its main signal runs through Gs, adenylyl cyclase, cAMP, and protein kinase A, which increase iodide uptake, thyroglobulin and thyroid peroxidase expression, hormone release, and growth of follicular cells. At high TSH levels the receptor can also engage Gq, but cAMP is the main pathway. The same Gs/cAMP pathway is used by ACTH, LH, FSH, PTH, and glucagon. Chronic TSH stimulation is why iodine deficiency and dyshormonogenesis cause goiter.
whyNot: Receptors with intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity bind insulin and IGF-1.
JAK/STAT signaling is used by growth hormone and prolactin, whose receptors are cytokine-type receptors without their own kinase.
Gq with IP3 and calcium is the main pathway for TRH, GnRH, and oxytocin. TSH uses it only at high concentrations.
Correct.

questions.stem: After levothyroxine is started, T3 formed in her developing brain binds receptors that regulate genes needed for myelination. Which of the following best describes how this receptor controls its target genes?
options: It binds cAMP response elements after phosphorylation by protein kinase A
It moves from cytoplasm to nucleus after heat shock proteins are released
It pairs with the retinoid X receptor on response elements in DNA
It activates JAK kinases that phosphorylate STAT transcription factors
approach: T3 enters cells through membrane transporters such as MCT8 and reaches the nucleus.
The thyroid hormone receptor belongs to the nuclear receptor family and is a DNA-binding transcription factor.
It binds DNA as a heterodimer with the retinoid X receptor (RXR) at thyroid hormone response elements.
questions.why: Thyroid hormone receptors sit in the nucleus already bound to DNA. They usually pair with the retinoid X receptor, and the pair attaches to thyroid hormone response elements near target genes. Without hormone, the receptor holds corepressors that silence the gene. When T3 binds, the corepressors leave and coactivators are recruited, which switches transcription on. This is how T3 controls genes for myelin proteins, neuronal growth, and Na/K-ATPase.
whyNot: CREB binds cAMP response elements after protein kinase A phosphorylates it. This is the pathway of Gs-coupled hormones such as TSH and glucagon.
Glucocorticoid receptors wait in the cytoplasm bound to heat shock proteins and enter the nucleus once hormone binds. Thyroid hormone receptors are already in the nucleus.
Correct.
JAK/STAT signaling is used by growth hormone, prolactin, and cytokines acting on membrane receptors.

case: A 24-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-day history of a painful swelling in the front of her neck that began after a cold. She has had a small painless lump in the same place since childhood. Temperature is 38.2 °C (100.8 °F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a 2.5-cm tender, erythematous, fluctuant mass in the midline of the neck just below the hyoid bone. The mass moves upward when she swallows and when she protrudes her tongue. Leukocyte count is 14,200/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000). Ultrasonography shows a thick-walled midline cyst containing debris and a normally located thyroid gland. Serum TSH concentration is normal. Diagnosis: infected thyroglossal duct cyst.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why the mass moves upward when she protrudes her tongue?
options: It lies within the pretracheal fascia around the thyroid
It arises from remnants of the second pharyngeal cleft
It is attached to the sternocleidomastoid by fascia
Its tract connects to the foramen cecum of the tongue
approach: A midline cyst near the hyoid bone that has been present since childhood suggests a thyroglossal duct cyst.
The cyst is a leftover piece of the duct along which the thyroid descended from the foramen cecum of the tongue.
Its tract stays linked to the hyoid bone and the base of the tongue, so tongue protrusion pulls it upward.
questions.why: The thyroglossal duct normally disappears after the thyroid reaches the neck. If a segment persists, its epithelium secretes fluid and forms a cyst anywhere from the base of the tongue to the thyroid, most often near or just below the hyoid bone. The tract runs close to, and often through, the hyoid and connects up to the foramen cecum. Tongue protrusion pulls on this tract, so the cyst rises. Because the tract can open into the oral cavity, mouth bacteria can infect the cyst, often after an upper respiratory infection, which is the most common complication.
whyNot: Pretracheal fascia explains why thyroid masses rise with swallowing. It does not explain movement with tongue protrusion, which needs a link to the tongue.
Second pharyngeal cleft remnants form branchial cleft cysts in the lateral neck along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid.
A fascial attachment to the sternocleidomastoid would tie a lateral mass to that muscle. It would not move with the tongue.
Correct.

questions.stem: After the infection resolves, excision of the cyst and its tract is planned. Before surgery, the surgeon confirms by imaging that a thyroid gland is present in its normal position. Which of the following is the main reason for this step?
options: The cyst may be the only thyroid tissue present
The cyst may open into a pyriform sinus fistula
The cyst may be a lateral branchial cleft cyst
The cyst may compress the recurrent laryngeal nerve
approach: Thyroid tissue can stop anywhere along the path of descent.
In a few patients, a midline mass along the thyroglossal tract is ectopic thyroid and the neck has no other thyroid.
Removing it would leave the patient permanently hypothyroid, so a normal gland must be confirmed first.
questions.why: A midline mass along the thyroglossal tract is usually a simple cyst, but it can be ectopic thyroid tissue, and sometimes that tissue is the patient's only thyroid. Ultrasonography or a thyroid scan confirms a normal gland before surgery. Its location also tells it apart from a branchial cleft cyst. A thyroglossal duct cyst is in the midline and moves with swallowing and tongue protrusion. A second branchial cleft cyst lies laterally along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid and does not move with the tongue.
whyNot: Correct.
A pyriform sinus fistula is a third or fourth pouch remnant that causes recurrent infection in the left thyroid lobe. It is not part of the thyroglossal tract.
Her mass is in the midline and moves with the tongue. A branchial cleft cyst is lateral, and examination already rules it out.
The recurrent laryngeal nerves run in the tracheoesophageal grooves, away from a midline cyst near the hyoid bone.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman had a midline neck mass removed 6 months ago without preoperative imaging. Pathologic examination showed normal thyroid follicles, and she has no other thyroid tissue. She now has amenorrhea and a milky nipple discharge. Her serum TSH concentration is 62 μU/mL (0.4 to 4.0), free T4 concentration is 0.3 ng/dL (0.8 to 1.8), and prolactin concentration is 48 ng/mL (less than 25). Which of the following best explains her increased prolactin concentration?
options: A prolactin-secreting adenoma of the anterior pituitary
Reduced renal clearance of circulating prolactin
Excess TRH acting on pituitary lactotrophs
Estrogen-induced growth of pituitary lactotrophs
approach: Read the thyroid tests: high TSH with low free T4 is primary hypothyroidism, here caused by removal of her only thyroid tissue.
Low thyroid hormone removes feedback on the hypothalamus, so TRH secretion rises.
TRH stimulates lactotrophs as well as thyrotrophs. Prolactin rises and suppresses GnRH, causing amenorrhea and galactorrhea.
questions.why: In primary hypothyroidism, TSH is high and free T4 is low. In central hypothyroidism, free T4 is low but TSH is low or inappropriately normal. A TSH-secreting adenoma gives high TSH with high free T4. Here, the loss of thyroid hormone raises hypothalamic TRH, and TRH also stimulates prolactin release. Raised prolactin inhibits GnRH pulses, so LH and FSH fall, which causes menstrual disturbance and infertility. Thyroid hormone replacement lowers TRH and corrects the prolactin level, so thyroid function should be checked in anyone with hyperprolactinemia.
whyNot: A prolactinoma can cause the same reproductive symptoms, but it does not explain her high TSH and low free T4. Her thyroid loss accounts for everything.
Kidney failure reduces prolactin clearance, but nothing suggests kidney disease here.
Correct.
High estrogen, as in pregnancy, enlarges lactotrophs. She has amenorrhea from suppressed gonadotropins, so her estrogen is likely low.

questions.stem: Needle aspiration of the infected cyst yields pus. Culture grows gram-positive cocci in chains that are catalase-negative, beta-hemolytic, and sensitive to bacitracin. Which of the following organisms is most likely?
options: Staphylococcus aureus
Streptococcus pyogenes
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Haemophilus influenzae
approach: Gram-positive cocci in chains that are catalase-negative are streptococci.
Beta-hemolysis with bacitracin sensitivity identifies group A Streptococcus.
Group A Streptococcus, Staphylococcus aureus, and Streptococcus pneumoniae are the classic causes of bacterial neck and thyroid infections.
questions.why: Bacterial infections of the thyroid region, including acute suppurative thyroiditis and infected developmental cysts, are most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, and Streptococcus pneumoniae, with oral anaerobes in some cases. Laboratory features tell them apart. Streptococcus pyogenes is a catalase-negative, beta-hemolytic coccus in chains that is sensitive to bacitracin. Infection often follows an upper respiratory illness, when organisms from the pharynx reach a tract that opens into the mouth or pharynx.
whyNot: Staphylococcus aureus forms clusters and is catalase-positive and coagulase-positive.
Correct.
Streptococcus pneumoniae is a lancet-shaped diplococcus that is alpha-hemolytic, optochin-sensitive, and bile-soluble.
Haemophilus influenzae is a small gram-negative coccobacillus that needs factors X and V to grow.

topics: Bacteria in thyroid and neck infections

dx: Acute suppurative thyroiditis from a pyriform sinus fistula
case: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of a 3-day history of fever, pain on swallowing, and a painful swelling on the left side of the anterior neck. She had a similar episode 1 year ago. Temperature is 39.0 °C (102.2 °F), pulse is 124/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a warm, red, tender, fluctuant swelling over the left lobe of the thyroid gland. Leukocyte count is 18,500/mm3 (4,500 to 13,500), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 62 mm/h (0 to 20). Serum TSH and free T4 concentrations are within the reference ranges. Ultrasonography shows an abscess in the left thyroid lobe. A later barium swallow shows a sinus tract from the left pyriform sinus. Diagnosis: acute suppurative thyroiditis from a pyriform sinus fistula.

questions.stem: Needle aspiration of the left thyroid lobe is performed. Which of the following is most likely to be seen in the aspirate?
options: Lymphocytes, plasma cells, and Hürthle cells
Neutrophils and gram-positive cocci
Multinucleated giant cells around colloid
Atypical follicular cells with nuclear grooves
approach: Put the findings together: high fever, leukocytosis, a red, fluctuant gland, an abscess on ultrasound, and normal thyroid function.
This is a bacterial infection of the thyroid, so the aspirate is pus.
Pus contains neutrophils and the causative bacteria, most often gram-positive cocci such as Staphylococcus aureus or streptococci.
questions.why: Acute suppurative thyroiditis is a bacterial infection that forms an abscess in the gland. Patients have fever and a painful, tender, sometimes fluctuant swelling, often with pain on swallowing. Thyroid function is usually normal because the infection is localized and most of the gland keeps working. This helps separate it from subacute thyroiditis, which usually causes thyrotoxicosis. The thyroid normally resists infection because of its capsule, rich blood supply and lymphatic drainage, and high iodine content, so a recurrent left-sided infection in a child suggests a pyriform sinus fistula.
whyNot: Lymphocytes, plasma cells, and Hürthle cells are found in Hashimoto thyroiditis, which is painless and causes no fever.
Correct.
Giant cells around colloid are found in subacute granulomatous thyroiditis, which causes pain and fever but no abscess and usually causes thyrotoxicosis.
Nuclear grooves in atypical follicular cells suggest papillary carcinoma, which does not cause fever or a fluctuant swelling.

questions.stem: Her sinus tract is a remnant of the fourth pharyngeal pouch. Which of the following structures normally develops from this same pouch?
options: Inferior parathyroid glands
Thymus
Palatine tonsil crypt epithelium
Superior parathyroid glands
approach: Recall the pouch derivatives: second pouch, palatine tonsil; third pouch, thymus and inferior parathyroids; fourth pouch, superior parathyroids.
The structures from the third pouch travel farther down with the thymus, past the fourth pouch structures.
This is why third pouch glands end up as the inferior parathyroids, and why the superior glands come from the fourth pouch.
questions.why: The third pharyngeal pouch forms the thymus and the inferior parathyroid glands. As the thymus migrates into the chest, it pulls these parathyroids down past the fourth pouch glands, so third pouch glands end up inferior. They may also be pulled too far, into the thymus or anterior mediastinum. The fourth pouch forms the superior parathyroid glands, which stay closer to their origin and are more constant in position. Parafollicular C cells come from neural crest cells that enter the ultimobranchial body, a derivative of the most caudal pouch. A pyriform sinus fistula is a remnant of the third or fourth pouch, and it is usually on the left.
whyNot: The inferior parathyroid glands come from the third pouch and descend with the thymus. This is why ectopic inferior parathyroids are found in the mediastinum.
The thymus develops from the third pouch.
The epithelium of the palatine tonsil develops from the second pouch.
Correct.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy on the same ward has a craniopharyngioma and has fatigue and slowed growth. His free T4 concentration is 0.6 ng/dL (0.8 to 1.8), TSH concentration is 1.1 μU/mL (0.7 to 5.7), and prolactin concentration is 42 ng/mL (less than 20). After an intravenous injection of TRH, his serum TSH concentration rises. Which of the following is the most likely site of the defect causing his low free T4 concentration?
options: Hypothalamus
Anterior pituitary
Thyroid gland
Peripheral tissue deiodinases
approach: Low free T4 with a TSH that is not raised means the problem is above the thyroid (central hypothyroidism).
TSH rises after TRH injection, so the pituitary thyrotrophs can still respond. The missing signal is TRH from the hypothalamus.
Raised prolactin supports this, because loss of hypothalamic dopamine releases lactotrophs from inhibition.
questions.why: A failing thyroid would remove feedback and raise TSH, so his normal TSH with low free T4 points to the pituitary or hypothalamus. The TRH injection separates the two. Pituitary thyrotrophs that respond to TRH are working, so the missing piece is TRH from the hypothalamus. Prolactin is the one pituitary hormone mainly held down by the hypothalamus, through dopamine. When a craniopharyngioma damages the hypothalamus or stalk, prolactin rises while the other pituitary hormones fall. TSH in hypothalamic hypothyroidism may be normal in the assay but has less biological activity.
whyNot: Correct.
Pituitary thyrotroph failure would give little or no TSH rise after TRH, and would not explain a raised prolactin.
Primary thyroid failure would raise TSH well above the reference range.
Deiodinase defects change T3 production. They would not lower free T4 with an inappropriately normal TSH.

questions.stem: She later undergoes excision of the sinus tract with partial left thyroidectomy. After surgery, her voice is weak and breathy, and laryngoscopy shows that the left vocal fold does not move. Injury to which of the following nerves most likely explains these findings?
options: External branch of the left superior laryngeal nerve
Internal branch of the left superior laryngeal nerve
Left recurrent laryngeal nerve
Left ansa cervicalis
approach: A vocal fold that does not move means loss of the muscles that open and close the glottis.
All intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs in the tracheoesophageal groove, right behind the thyroid lobe, close to the inferior thyroid artery, so it is at risk in thyroid surgery.
questions.why: The recurrent laryngeal nerve climbs in the tracheoesophageal groove, passes close to the branches of the inferior thyroid artery behind the thyroid lobe, and enters the larynx. It supplies every intrinsic laryngeal muscle except the cricothyroid, including the posterior cricoarytenoid, the only muscle that opens the vocal folds. Injury on one side leaves that fold fixed and the voice weak and breathy. Injury on both sides can narrow the airway enough to cause stridor. The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery, and its injury only weakens high-pitched sounds.
whyNot: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies the cricothyroid, which tenses the fold. Injury reduces vocal pitch and projection, but the fold still moves.
The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve gives sensation above the vocal folds. Injury raises aspiration risk but does not paralyze the fold.
Correct.
The ansa cervicalis supplies the infrahyoid strap muscles. Injury has little effect and does not affect the vocal folds.

dx: Papillary thyroid carcinoma with postoperative hypocalcemia
case: A 36-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a painless lump in her neck. At age 8 years, she received radiation therapy to the neck for Hodgkin lymphoma. Physical examination shows a firm, 2-cm nodule in the right thyroid lobe and a firm, enlarged right cervical lymph node. Serum TSH concentration is normal. Ultrasonography shows a hypoechoic nodule with microcalcifications. She undergoes total thyroidectomy with central neck dissection, which confirms papillary thyroid carcinoma with lymph node metastases. On the second postoperative day, she has numbness around the mouth and tingling in her fingers. Tapping over the facial nerve causes twitching of the facial muscles. Serum calcium concentration is 7.1 mg/dL (8.5 to 10.2), albumin concentration is 4.0 g/dL (3.5 to 5.0), and PTH concentration is 6 pg/mL (10 to 65). Diagnosis: papillary thyroid carcinoma with postoperative hypoparathyroidism.

questions.stem: Microscopic examination of her thyroid tumor is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Uniform follicles with invasion through the tumor capsule
Nests of polygonal cells in a stroma rich in amyloid
Clear, overlapping nuclei with grooves and psammoma bodies
Sheets of pleomorphic spindle cells and bizarre giant cells
approach: Use the clues: a young woman, childhood neck radiation, microcalcifications, and spread to cervical lymph nodes point to papillary carcinoma.
Papillary carcinoma is diagnosed mainly by its nuclear features.
Look for clear (Orphan Annie eye) nuclei, nuclear grooves, and psammoma bodies, which show up as microcalcifications on ultrasound.
questions.why: Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer, and childhood radiation to the neck is its best-known risk factor. The diagnosis rests on the nuclei: they look empty and clear (Orphan Annie eye nuclei), overlap, and show grooves and pseudoinclusions. Laminated calcified psammoma bodies are common. The tumor spreads mainly through lymphatics to cervical nodes. Even with nodal spread, most patients do very well after surgery, with 10-year survival above 90%.
whyNot: Capsular invasion by a follicular tumor with uniform nuclei defines follicular carcinoma, which spreads through blood rather than lymph.
Polygonal or spindle cells in an amyloid stroma are medullary carcinoma, which arises from C cells and secretes calcitonin.
Correct.
Bizarre spindle and giant cells describe anaplastic carcinoma, a rapidly fatal tumor of older adults.

questions.stem: Molecular testing of her tumor is performed. Which of the following genetic alterations is most likely, given her history?
options: RET/PTC gene rearrangement
PAX8-PPARG gene fusion
Germline RET point mutation
Inactivating TP53 mutation
approach: Identify the tumor: papillary carcinoma after childhood radiation.
Ionizing radiation causes double-strand DNA breaks, and faulty repair joins pieces of different genes.
In the thyroid, this most often fuses the RET kinase domain to a partner gene (RET/PTC), which activates MAP kinase signaling.
questions.why: Papillary carcinomas are driven by activation of the MAP kinase pathway. In sporadic tumors, the most common change is the BRAF V600E point mutation. In tumors that follow radiation, as seen in children after the Chernobyl accident, RET/PTC rearrangements are much more common. These fusions place the RET tyrosine kinase domain under the promoter of a partner gene that is always expressed in follicular cells, so the kinase is switched on all the time. Follicular carcinomas tend to carry RAS mutations or PAX8-PPARG fusions, and medullary carcinomas carry RET point mutations.
whyNot: Correct.
PAX8-PPARG fusion is typical of follicular carcinoma.
Germline activating RET point mutations cause MEN 2A and 2B, with medullary carcinoma of the C cells.
TP53 loss is found in anaplastic carcinoma and marks progression to an aggressive tumor.

questions.stem: During surgery, the surgeon finds both superior parathyroid glands easily on the back of the upper thyroid lobes but has to search for the inferior glands. Which of the following best explains this difference?
options: Fixed location inside the carotid sheath
Variable location near the lower thyroid poles
Location on the anterior surface of the isthmus
Location above the thyroid beside the hyoid bone
approach: The parathyroids usually lie on the posterior surface of the thyroid lobes, two on each side.
The superior glands are fairly constant, near the level of the cricoid cartilage.
The inferior glands are more variable. They may sit near the lower pole, in the thyrothymic ligament or thymus, or in the mediastinum.
questions.why: The superior parathyroids lie in a fairly constant spot on the back of the upper part of each lobe. The inferior parathyroids have a longer embryonic path, so their position varies more. They are usually near the lower pole, but they can lie in fat around the lower pole, inside the thymus, or in the mediastinum. Surgeons must look for them carefully, because removing them by mistake or cutting off their blood supply causes hypoparathyroidism. Central neck dissection works in the same area, which raises the risk.
whyNot: The carotid sheath holds the carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve. The parathyroids are not inside it.
Correct.
Parathyroid glands lie on the posterior surface of the lobes.
Glands that fail to descend can rarely lie high in the neck, but that is the exception. The inferior glands normally sit low.

questions.stem: Her surgeon reports that all four parathyroid glands were identified and left in place. Interruption of which of the following vessels close to the thyroid capsule is the most likely cause of her hypocalcemia?
options: Superior thyroid artery at the upper pole
Thyroid ima artery at the isthmus
Middle thyroid vein at the lateral border
Inferior thyroid artery branches
approach: Read the labs: low calcium with low PTH and normal albumin after thyroid surgery means hypoparathyroidism.
The glands were left in place, so their blood supply must have been cut.
Both the superior and inferior parathyroid glands depend mainly on the inferior thyroid artery, whose branches are divided during thyroidectomy.
questions.why: The parathyroid glands are small and get blood from tiny end branches. Most of this blood, for both upper and lower glands, comes from the inferior thyroid artery. When the surgeon ligates its branches close to the thyroid capsule, glands left in place can lose their blood supply and stop making PTH. Without PTH, calcium falls within a day or two, causing perioral numbness, tingling, and the Chvostek sign. The problem is often temporary if the glands recover their blood supply. Accidental removal of parathyroid tissue causes the same picture.
whyNot: The superior thyroid artery can add a little blood to the superior glands, but it is not the main parathyroid supply.
The thyroid ima artery is present in only a few people and supplies the isthmus, away from the parathyroids.
The middle thyroid vein drains blood away from the gland. Ligating it does not cut off the arterial supply to the parathyroids.
Correct.

dx: Follicular thyroid carcinoma with bone metastasis
case: A 63-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of worsening pain in his right hip. He has had a slowly enlarging lump in his neck for 2 years. Physical examination shows a firm, 4-cm nodule in the left thyroid lobe and no cervical lymphadenopathy. Serum TSH and calcium concentrations are normal. X-ray of the pelvis shows a lytic lesion in the right ilium. Biopsy of the bone lesion shows follicles that contain colloid, and the tumor cells stain for thyroglobulin. He undergoes total thyroidectomy, and pathologic examination confirms the diagnosis. Diagnosis: follicular thyroid carcinoma with bone metastasis.

questions.stem: Fine-needle aspiration of his thyroid nodule before surgery showed only follicular cells and could not separate adenoma from carcinoma. Which of the following findings in the resected tumor establishes that it is a carcinoma?
options: Tumor cells inside capsular blood vessels
Crowded microfollicles with very little colloid
Nuclear grooves with intranuclear inclusions
Frequent mitotic figures among tumor cells
approach: Follicular adenoma and follicular carcinoma can look identical cell by cell.
The only reliable difference is invasion: through the full thickness of the capsule or into blood vessels.
That is why aspiration cytology cannot make the call, and the whole capsule must be examined after surgery.
questions.why: Follicular adenomas and carcinomas are both encapsulated nodules of follicular cells with similar nuclei. Carcinoma is diagnosed when tumor cells invade through the capsule or into vessels in or beyond the capsule. Vascular invasion also explains how follicular carcinoma spreads: through the blood, to bone and lung, while lymph node spread is uncommon. Bone metastases are usually lytic, as in this patient. Because the metastases often keep follicular function, they may make thyroglobulin and take up iodine.
whyNot: Correct.
Microfollicles with scant colloid occur in both adenoma and carcinoma, so they cannot separate the two.
Nuclear grooves and pseudoinclusions are features of papillary carcinoma, not follicular carcinoma.
Mitoses can occur in both benign and malignant follicular tumors and do not define carcinoma.

questions.stem: After thyroidectomy, his bone metastasis is treated with radioactive iodine-131 while his TSH concentration is raised. The uptake of this isotope by the metastatic cells depends most directly on which of the following?
options: Thyroid peroxidase at the apical membrane
Pendrin chloride-iodide exchanger at the apical side
Sodium-iodide symporter on the basal membrane
Megalin-mediated uptake of thyroglobulin
approach: Radioactive iodine works only if tumor cells pull iodide in from the blood the way normal follicular cells do.
The first step of thyroid hormone synthesis is active iodide uptake by the sodium-iodide symporter on the basolateral membrane.
TSH increases symporter expression, which is why TSH is raised before treatment.
questions.why: The sodium-iodide symporter on the basolateral membrane uses the sodium gradient to bring two sodium ions and one iodide ion into the cell, concentrating iodide many times above plasma levels. Well-differentiated follicular carcinoma cells often keep this transporter, so they take up iodine-131, and its beta radiation destroys them. TSH increases symporter expression, so TSH is raised by stopping thyroid hormone or by giving recombinant TSH before treatment. The later steps are pendrin moving iodide into the lumen, thyroid peroxidase oxidizing and attaching it, and proteolysis of thyroglobulin to release hormone.
whyNot: Thyroid peroxidase oxidizes and organifies iodide after it enters the cell. It helps keep iodine in the cell but does not bring it in.
Pendrin moves iodide out of the cell into the follicular lumen. It acts after uptake.
Correct.
Megalin is a receptor that takes thyroglobulin back from the lumen. It does not carry free iodide in from the blood.

questions.stem: Tumor cells from the lower part of the left lobe entered the inferior thyroid veins before reaching the systemic circulation. These veins drain most directly into which of the following?
options: Internal jugular veins
External jugular veins
Subclavian veins
Brachiocephalic veins
approach: Follicular carcinoma spreads through the blood, so trace its venous route.
The superior and middle thyroid veins drain into the internal jugular vein.
The inferior thyroid veins run down in front of the trachea into the brachiocephalic veins, and from there to the superior vena cava, right heart, lungs, and systemic circulation.
questions.why: The thyroid drains through three pairs of veins. The superior and middle thyroid veins empty into the internal jugular veins. The inferior thyroid veins come from the lower poles and isthmus, often form a plexus in front of the trachea, and drain into the left and right brachiocephalic veins. Tumor cells that invade these veins reach the lungs first and can then reach the bones. This explains the typical metastatic sites of follicular carcinoma.
whyNot: The internal jugular veins receive the superior and middle thyroid veins.
The external jugular veins drain the scalp and face and do not receive thyroid veins.
The subclavian veins drain the upper limb and join the internal jugular veins to form the brachiocephalic veins.
Correct.

questions.stem: After treatment, he takes levothyroxine once each morning. His serum T4 concentration stays nearly constant between doses. Which of the following best explains this stability?
options: Rapid uptake of T4 into colloid stores
Binding of over 99% of T4 to plasma proteins
Slow absorption of T4 from the gut over several days
Continuous recycling of T4 through the bile
approach: Ask why a once-daily dose gives a steady level: the hormone must be cleared slowly.
More than 99% of T4 is bound to thyroxine-binding globulin, transthyretin, and albumin, and only free hormone is metabolized or enters cells.
The bound pool acts as a large reservoir, so T4 has a half-life of about 7 days.
questions.why: Only the free fraction of thyroid hormone enters cells, binds receptors, and is broken down. For T4, this free fraction is very small, about 0.03%. The rest is bound mainly to thyroxine-binding globulin, with smaller amounts on transthyretin and albumin. The bound pool refills the free pool as hormone is used, so T4 has a half-life of about 7 days. A daily dose then adds only a small amount to a large, steady pool. T3 is less tightly bound and has a half-life of about 1 day.
whyNot: Colloid storage happens only in thyroid follicles, and his thyroid has been removed.
Correct.
Levothyroxine is absorbed in the small intestine within a few hours.
Some T4 conjugates are excreted in bile and partly reabsorbed, but this is a small effect and does not explain the long half-life.
